stem: A57-year-old man is reviewed in the Cardiology Clinic following a third myocardial infarction(MI) over the past 18 months. He continues to smoke five cigarettes per day and takes bisoprolol, ramipril, high-dose atorvastatin, aspirin and clopidogrel. His blood pressure(BP) is 110/80 mmHg and pulse is 64 bpm and regular. His chest is clear and heart sounds are normal. There is no ankle swelling. Investigation Result Normal value Haemoglobin(Hb) 145 g/l 135-175 g/lL White cell count (WCC) 7.0×10/L 4-11×10/L Platelets(PLT) 181×10/L 150-400×10/L Sodium (Na+) 142 mmol/L 135-145 mmol/L Potassium(K+) 4.3 mmol/L 3.5-5.0 mmol/l Creatinine (Cr) 119μmol/L 50-120 μmol/l Low-density lipoprotein (LDL) cholesterol 4.1 mmol/l 1.8 mmol/l High-density lipoprotein(HDL) 1.2 mmol/L 1.6 mmol/L Triglycerides 1.3 mmol/L 1.7 mmol/L Which of the following is the most useful intervention in this patient?
explanation: Evolocumab binds proprotein convertase subtilisin/kexin type 9(PCSK9) and prevents it from binding to low- density lipoprotein (LDL) receptors on the liver surface. This enhances the ability of the liver to bind LDL cholesterol and remove it from circulation. On top of statin, it reduces LDL cholesterol by approximately 60% and reduces major adverse cardiovascular events by around 15%.The National Institute for Health and Care Excellence(NICE) guidelines allow use where LDL is persistently above 4.0 mmol/l despite maximally tolerated lipid-Lowering therapy. Given this is the patient's third Ml in a short period, it is appropriate to move to this rather than ezetimibe as an intermediate step. explanations.

stem: A 73-year-old man is reviewed on the Medical Admissions Ward after suffering a complex partial seizure. A decision is made to start him on carbamazepine. He is also taking long-term warfarin therapy, having been diagnosed with atrial fibrillation four years ago. Which of the following is the most likely to happen to this patient's international normalised ratio (INR)?
options: Fall in his INR maximal over 3-4 weeks
Fall in his INR maximal over 2-3 days
Rise in his INR maximal over 3-4 weeks
Rise in his INR maximal over 2-3 days
explanation: Carbamazepine is a potent cytochrome P450 enzyme inducer across a range of P450 enzyme subfamilies, including 1A2,2B6,2C9,2C19 and 3A4.It also exhibits autoinduction, which builds over a number of weeks. This leads to a need to increase the dose for treating epilepsy after around three weeks. What this means in terms of INR is that the INR progressively falls because of a reduction in warfarin efficacy over the course of 3-4 weeks. Q.

stem: An 18-year-old man is referred to the Endocrine Clinic. He has failed to enter puberty. His only other medical problem is that he has no sense of smell. He is 1.7m in height; his blood pressure is 105/75mmHg and his pulse is 67 bpm and regular. His parents are completely well. His body mass index is 22 kg/m.He has small testes and almost absent pubic and axillary hair. Which of the following is the most likely inheritance of the patient's condition?
explanation: Most cases of Kallmann syndrome follow an X-Linked recessive pattern. It is caused by a mutation in the ANOS1 gene which is responsible for migration of olfactory neurones to their correct position. Failure of migration leads to absence of development of the olfactory bulb, lack of production of gonadotrophin- releasing hormone and subsequent failure to enter puberty because of a lack of luteinising hormone (LH) and follicle-stimulating hormone(FSH) production. It fits with the clinical picture described here. Puberty and fertility can be restored with pulsed administration of gonadotrophins. Q.

stem: A32-year-old man presents to the Emergency Department with left-sided pleuritic chest pain. He is not appreciably short of breath. He is a non-smoker. His blood pressure is 115/82 mmHg and his pulse is 68 bpm and regular. His chest appears clear on auscultation. A chest×-ray reveals a rim of air on the left-hand side measuring 1.5 cm at the level of the hilum side, consistent with a pneumothorax. Which of the following is the most appropriate next step?
options: Air aspiration and re-X-ray before discharge
Air aspiration and admit for high-flow oxygen
explanation: This patient has a small primary pneumothorax2 cm at the level of the hilum, with no symptoms of breathlessness. In this situation, discharge can be considered, with review in the Outpatient Department after a 2-to 4-week period. Q.

stem: An 84-year-old man who has suffered a large subarachnoid haemorrhage requires review. He is unconscious but has paroxysms of coughing, which appear to be due to excess secretions. He requires regular suctioning and his relatives are concerned that he may be uncomfortable when this is done. Which of the following is the most appropriate intervention?
explanation: Glycopyrronium is an anticholinergic that can be given subcutaneously every four hours to reduce respiratory secretions.In this situation, it is the most appropriate intervention. Hyoscine butylbromide or hyoscine hydrobromide are potential alternatives. Q.

stem: A 43-year-old woman who has primary ovarian failure and a previous left Colle's fracture is reviewed in the Medical Admissions Unit following a complex partial seizure.You are discussing options for treatment with her. Which of the following anti-seizure medications carries the most risk of reducing the patient's bone mineral density?
explanation: Of the class of anti-seizure medications,phenytoin is thought to carry the highest risk of osteoporosis associated with its use.In a prospective study of premenopausal women, use of the drug for one year was associated with a 2.6% reduction in bone mineral density at the femoral neck. It is thought that enzyme inducers such as phenytoin and carbamazepine carry a greater risk of osteoporosis overall than non-enzyme- inducing agents. This may be, in part, because of increased metabolism of sex steroids. Q.

stem: An 18-year-old man is admitted to the Emergency Department with a generalised erythematous maculopapular rash. He says he was ill for a few days before the rash began with symptoms of a cough, cold and conjunctivitis.You note small red spots, each with a bluish-white speck, on examination of the buccal mucosa. He tells you no one in the family has been vaccinated and others have had a similar illness. Which of the following is the most likely vector of transmission for this condition?
explanation: Measles is subject to airborne spread via respiratory droplets, which accounts for the fact it is so infectious. It fits with the presentation here-a prodromal coryzal illness and the development of a rash with the presence of Koplik's spots on examination of the buccal mucosa.Ribonucleic acid(RNA) detection in saliva can be used to confirm the diagnosis. Infection can have a poor outcome when, as on this occasion, it occurs in young adults. Q.

stem: An 18-year-old woman, who is in her final year of A-levels, presents to the Neurology Clinic following a single tonic-clonic seizure at home. According to her mother, she has been clumsy, particularly in the morning, over the past 2-3 years and is always spilling things on the breakfast table and knocking things over because of sudden jerks of her arms. She is doing well with her school work. Neurological examination is unremarkable. Which of the following is the most appropriate treatment for her seizures?
explanation: This patient's initial myoclonic jerks followed by a tonic-clonic seizure are suggestive of a diagnosis of juvenile myoclonic epilepsy. It may be associated with mood disorder, but patients with the condition usually have normal cognitive function. Treatment options include valproate, lamotrigine and levetiracetam. Levetiracetam is preferred because it is relatively safe should pregnancy occur and does not augment symptoms in some patients(unlike lamotrigine). Q.

stem: A 45-year-old nurse is reviewed in the Occupational Health Services Department following the results of a third hepatitis B vaccination. She has only mounted a very modest antibody response despite three vaccine injections. Which of the following cells is likely to give her long-lasting immunity to hepatitis B?
explanation: T cells are primarily responsible for immune memory and long-term protection from vaccination such as this one. They can co-ordinate the immune response by producing inflammatory cytokines and generating populations of cytotoxic T cells and stimulate the production of antigen-specific B cells against a particular pathogen. Regulatory T cells also dampen down the host immune response and prevent an autoimmune attack. Difficulty.

stem: You are investigating the potential to treat patients with non-alcoholic steatohepatitis using a thyroid hormone receptor agonist. Where do drugs need to be targeted to achieve receptor agonism?
explanation: The thyroid hormone receptor is a nuclear receptor that acts via a genomic and a non-genomic pathway. The non-genomic pathway is activated when T3 binds to the thyroid hormone receptor, which then leads to an increase in cyclic guanosine monophosphate (GMP). In turn, this leads to activation of cyclic GMP-dependent protein kinase, which has a positive effect on cell viability.The genomic pathway of thyroid hormone receptor activation regulates gene transcription. The receptor can regulate transcription as a monomer, but it also acts in tandem with other nuclear receptors such as the retinoid X receptor. Dificulty.

stem: A 23-year-old man with cerebral palsy presents to his General Practitioner, complaining of excessive drowsiness. His current medication includes baclofen for muscle spasms and contractures. Which of the following best describes the mode of action of baclofen?
explanation: Baclofen is a GABA derivative that is chemically unrelated to other antispastic agents. It depresses monosynaptic and polysynaptic reflex transmission, by agonist action at GABA-B-receptors. This, in turn, inhibits the release of the excitatory amino acids glutamate and aspartate. Neuromuscular transmission is unaffected by baclofen. The major benefits of baclofen stem from its ability to reduce painful flexor spasms and spontaneous clonus, thereby facilitating patient mobility. Difficulty.

stem: A39-year-old off-duty fireman is admitted to the Emergency Department after having rescued a small child from a house fire. He is thought to have inhaled a mix of carbon dioxide(CO) and carbon monoxide (CO). What do peripheral chemoreceptors do in CO poisoning?
options: Drive a decrease in ventilatory rate
Drive an increase in ventilatory rate
Drive an increase in depth of inspiration
Drive a decrease in depth of inspiration
explanation: Carbon monoxide levels do not impact the activity of peripheral chemoreceptors. In this situation, where there has been CO and CO inhalation after a fire, it is likely that any dyspnoea is stimulated by CO inhalation and central chemoreceptor activity. One possible driver for respiratory depression after a house fire can be the inhalation of cyanide fumes from burning soft furnishings. Difficulty.

stem: A72-year-old man is reviewed on the Elderly Care Ward to help assess his risk of pressure sores. His weight is stable. He is restless because of a urinary tract infection and is incontinent of urine. He has impaired glucose tolerance. His skin is dry to touch and his body mass index(BMI) is 32 kg/m. Which of the following has the greatest impact on the patient's risk of pressure sores?
explanation: Obesity carries a significant excess risk of pressure sores, according to the Waterlow score, the most widely used scoring system for pressure sore risk. An average BMI (20-24.9 kg/m) carries no excess risk and a score of 0;a BMI of 25-29.9 kg/m carries a score of 1 and a BMI of30 kg/m carries a score of 3.BMI below 20 kg/m carries the greatest risk of pressure scores, adding 3 to the Waterlow score. Aggregate scores of10 signify an increased risk of pressure sores;for 15+,the risk is classified as high;for 20+,it is classified as very high. Difficulty.

stem: A 56-year-old man is reviewed in the clinic following a recent endoscopy and gastric biopsy for an upper gastrointestinal (GI) bleed. He enjoys spicy food, drinks three pints of beer per week and smokes five cigarettes per day. He has previous rheumatoid arthritis but takes no medication for this now. The biopsy reveals extensive lymphoid infiltration, with the formation of germinal centres within the lamina propria. Which of the following is the most likely cause of the biopsy changes?
explanation: The intense lymphoid infiltration seen here is suggestive of a gastric MALToma. MALTomas are strongly associated with chronic H.pylori infection. It is thought that antigenic stimulation over time as a result of H. pylorileads to the development of the lymphoma tissue. Eradication treatment for H.pylori can lead to resolution of the lesions and is the initial treatment of choice in all patients with MALToma who are H.pylori positive. Dificulty.

She continues to smoke five cigarettes per day. Her blood pressure is 105/80 mmHg and her pulse is 105 bpm and regular. She is pale and sweating. Her chest is clear and her abdomen is soft and non-tender. Her ankles are not swollen. Investigation Result Normal value Haemoglobin (Hb) 102 g/l 115-160 g/l White cell count(WCC) 11.4×10/L 4-11×10/L Platelets (PLT) 201×10/L 150-400×10/L Sodium(Na+) 143 mmol/L 135-145 mmol/L Potassium (K+) 4.0 mmol/L 3.5-5.0 mmol/L Creatinine (Cr) 110μmol/L 50-120 μmol/L Electrocardiogram 3 mm ST elevation in leads II, II and aVF High-sensitivity (hs) troponin T 125 ng/l 14 ng/l Which of the following is the most appropriate intervention?
explanation: This patient has clear ST elevation in the inferior leads, a marked elevation in troponin and symptoms consistent with an inferior MI. Percutaneous coronary intervention is, therefore, the optimal next step. Although coronary artery dissection is more common in pregnancy, occlusion is potentially more likely here, given the patient's tobacco smoking and the fact that pregnancy itself is a hypercoagulable state. Total coronary artery thrombosis is thought to be responsible for a presentation with Ml in up to 17% of pregnancy-related cases. Acute Coronary Syndrome and Myocardial Infarction explanations.

stem: A 32-year-old South-Asian woman presents to the clinic for review. She complains of chronic bone pain and weakness of her hips, which makes it difficult for her to climb the stairs. She follows a vegetarian diet and rarely leaves the house. Her blood pressure is 148/84 mmHg and her pulse is 84 bpm and regular. Her body mass index is 27 kg/m. She has a 4/5 weakness of her hip flexors. Investigations: Investigation Result Normal value Haemoglobin(Hb) 100 g/l 115-155 g/l White cell count (WCC) 6.1×109/L 4-11×10/L Platelets(PLT) 209×10/L 150-400×10/L Sodium (Na+) 144 mmol/L 135-145 mmol/L Potassium(K+) 4.3 mmol/L 3.5-5.0 mmol/L Creatinine (Cr) 102 μmol/L 50-120 μmol/L Calcium 2.1 mmol/L 2.1-2.65 mmol/L Phosphate(PO) 0.7 mmol/L 0.8-1.5 mmol/L Alkaline phosphatase 210 IU/L 30-130 IU/L Parathyroid hormone 130 ng/l 12-72 ng/l Which of the following is the most likely cause of her proximal muscle weakness?

Coupled with limited time spent outside, this has led to low vitamin D,a calcium level at the lower end of the normal range, low phosphate and raised alkaline phosphatase, with a reactiveincrease in parathyroid hormone. This clinical picture is consistent with osteomalacia. Calcium and vitamin D supplementation should lead to the resolution of the patient's symptoms. stem: A74-year-old man is reviewed in the Haematology Clinic after multiple transient ischaemic attacks(TIAs) in the last three months. On further questioning,it transpires he has suffered multiple headaches over the last five months. He has hypertension and suffered an inferior myocardial infarction some four years earlier. His blood pressure is 155/92 mmHg and his pulse is 84 bpm and regular. He has no residual neurological deficit. You note a petechial rash on skin examination.
